why: Reads like a long-form magazine feature (LRB / New Yorker register). Plausible as an authentic ELF long text, though at the demanding end of the range.

The physics is not just plausible, it is right: nucleating a fresh crystal needing roughly half again the vapour of maintaining one is real, and it does the argumentative work of explaining why the layers are invisible. That makes Q2 answerable from two independent places in the text.
Q3 hinges on a genuine two-effects-cancel point; C ('cools the ground instead') is a well-built trap for a reader who half-remembers the daylight clause.

Q4 is the best question here: A inverts the actual statistic (all 141 flew through a forecast layer; fewer than half left a mark), and getting to C requires carrying the over-forecasting finding across to the descents that were flown. Demanding but single-answer.

Q5 is settled by 'the satellite count is the smallest thing those two winters produced' plus the note that the second finding 'needed no picture at all'. D overstates (he never calls for ending the imagery) and B misreads the noncommittal 'Perhaps it would'.

The final paragraph is the densest stretch in the unit. The sentence 'only one of the readings it allows blames the forecast; two are the camera's, and the fourth is the success' asks the reader to count back to the four causes of an empty frame listed a few lines earlier; I had to re-read it once. It resolves correctly and is stylistically deliberate, but it is where friction lives.

Textkomplettering done properly: the passage is a real piece of writing first and a gap exercise second, with a genuine idea in it (the room runs on trust, the locked drawer does not, and nobody has had to decide whether that is a contradiction).
British register is consistent throughout (bin bag, saleroom, the number 14, crime number, pounds, 'honour' spelling in an option). No transatlantic slippage.

Gaps 2, 3 and 5 turn on fixed collocations ('give it up for lost', 'take them at their word', 'a foregone conclusion'); each has exactly one idiomatic filler and the alternatives are near-miss nouns rather than nonsense, which is the right difficulty shape.

Gap 1 is the one that rewards reading the logic rather than the phrase: the clearing schedule follows from nobody bothering to reclaim an umbrella, so it is a consequence, not a contrast, which rules out 'Conversely'.
Gap 4 is anchored by the preceding 'At the drawer it is not' and needs the reader to see that the questions must get harder, not softer; 'searching' is the only option that does that.
'the coat goes back across the counter' introduces a coat with no specific antecedent, but clothing is established in the first paragraph and it reads as a generic instance, not an error.
Short-text ELF format with a single question; the craftsman's voice (clipped, verbless closing fragments, 'Green oak throughout') is convincing and the byline fits it.

The engineering is correct, which matters for a first-time reader trying to build a mental picture: mitre gates meeting in a V pointing upstream so head pressure closes the joint, pair longer than the chamber is wide, thrust running through the leaf into the masonry.

The answer is secured by two consecutive sentences ('The pin is not fastened down' and 'beds its heel into the iron plate that lines the recess'), so the item does not depend on decoding the whole vocabulary load.

C is a genuinely good distractor because both halves are true individually but the causal link is wrong: the text attributes the shimming of the collar to hang and to the mitre posts meeting true, not to the pin carrying the weight. It cost me a second read to reject it, which is the right kind of difficulty.
Dense specialist vocabulary (heel post, mitre post, recess, shimmed, collar) is not glossed, but none of it is load-bearing for the question.
PARTIALLY (blind lean A). B is self-defeating on its face -- a pin that a leaf stands and swings on cannot be the thing
Compressed historical-commercial short text; the pre-decimal money and the pony-and-float detail carry the period without costume.

The arithmetic reconciles exactly, which is unusual and welcome: 168 divided by 21 gives eight weeks of takings, nine houses of a hundred and twenty are 1.575 a week, and eight weeks of that is 12.60, i.e. the 12 pounds 12 shillings refunded. A reader who checks is rewarded rather than tripped.

The key rests on an inference rather than a sentence: the thirteen-week clause is stated only as a protection inside that window, so the buyer necessarily absorbs later losses. Fair, and the sale of nine houses inside the window is the worked example that makes the rule legible.

A is the strongest distractor and is half-true; it is refuted by 'the round itself was reckoned in weeks of takings' rather than by house count. D is refuted by 'at the price the dairy fixed'. B is refuted by 'What the houses owed on the day of the change stayed the seller's to collect'. Each wrong option has a specific textual killer, which is the right construction.
Very high information density for its length, but nothing in it is decorative and every clause is used.
PARTIALLY. B is eliminable blind as a category confusion (houses on a milk round do not carry debts against them) and D
Reads like an authentic industrial-history LÄS text: concrete, period-appropriate register, glossary terms (sats, kubb, plån, brandstodsbolag) all genuinely needed and all glossed.

The chain of reasoning is clean and each question has exactly one defensible answer. Q1 depends on grasping why the paraffin comes before the sats (it holds the flame long enough for the wood to catch), which the third paragraph states plainly; the merchants' quote 'tände men slocknade' seals it.
Q4 is well built: D is directly refuted by 'Björk var det året billigare än asp. Det ändrade ingenting', and B is refuted by the 1938 machine change, leaving C.

Minor friction in one sentence: 'som anlades 1876 och från 1918 drevs inom ett större bolag, hämtade sitt virke inom en mil från fabriken ända fram till kriget' packs three dates in different directions (the war is later identified as WWI, i.e. before 1918). Nothing contradicts, but I re-read it once.

'Fyrtio gross björkstickor ... såldes ändå, till en uppköpare som aldrig hörde av sig' briefly reads as a contradiction (they were sold, so he did make contact) before landing as 'never contacted us again'. A wry incidental detail of the sort real HP texts do carry; not load-bearing for any question.
The internal numbers hang together (2,1 mm sticka in the old machine vs 1,9 mm in 1938 giving more sticks per kubb; 1911 trials, bath installed February 1912).
Convincing as a signed opinion piece by a driving instructor: first-person observation, a named source who pushes back, a concrete proposal at the end. The debattartikel voice is right for LÄS.
Q1 is clean arithmetic off the text (29 to 34 north of the school). C is properly refuted by the unchanged southern stretch and D by the Tunbergsvägen figure.

Q2 required holding two of the author's moves at once: she refuses a delay ('Jag begär ingen ny utredning, och jag tycker inte att nämnden ska vänta'), which kills A, and she argues the noise originates in braking and acceleration rather than in the rubber, which kills B. That leaves C and it is well earned.
The self-undercutting paragraph (Skedvall's three caveats, which the author concedes) is a nice authentic touch and makes the piece feel argued rather than asserted.
The closing offer to be proved wrong in April is a satisfying finish and does not create any second defensible reading of Q2.

Quiet essayistic voice, well sustained; the subject (teachers' handbooks for school wall charts) is exactly the sort of narrow cultural-history topic LÄS uses.

Q1 is a straight retrieval from the one sentence about history series ('Där dominerade beskeden redan i de tidigaste årgångarna'), and the three distractors are all unstated rather than half-true, so it is easy but fair.

Q2 is the harder one. D is drawn from Bråtemo's objection, which the author explicitly concedes is 'svårt att komma runt' before turning it aside with the parallel change in the charts themselves. A first-time reader who stops at the concession could be briefly tempted by D, but the 'Men' and the closing 1958 example (eleven statements, one question, placed last) make A clearly the best fit. Single defensible answer, but D is the live distractor.

Detail worth noting as good craft: the final booklet's one remaining question is about what the class has learned, i.e. a check rather than an opening, which quietly confirms the thesis without stating it.
